The pacing of the story feels very natural, appropriate, and balanced. For the most part, "story time" and "real world time" run nearly parallel, unfolding over just a few quiet minutes on the ferry at dusk. 

The writer uses slight **stretching of time** between lines of sparse dialogue—filling the silences with sensory details (the creeping fog, wiping the wet railing, looking across the river) and internal reflections. This slows the rhythm down, perfectly mirroring the quiet, melancholic atmosphere of the setting and the unspoken tension between mother and son. 

Conversely, a brief moment of **time compression** is used to summarize years of family history and loss in just three sentences (Jonas counting cars as a boy, Henning never wiping the chalk away, and the rain eventually washing it off). This seamlessly provides emotional depth and backstory without disrupting the grounded, real-time flow of the present scene.
